blocks.content: Chandigarh's polity chapter revolves around one structural peculiarity that generates most exam questions: it is administered by the Governor of Punjab, wearing a second hat as 'Administrator', rather than by its own dedicated Lieutenant Governor.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Chandigarh is administered as a Union Territory under Article 239 of the Constitution of India.
The Governor of Punjab serves as the ex-officio Administrator of the Union Territory of Chandigarh.
Local governance is administered by the Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh (MCC), created under the Punjab Municipal Corporation Act as extended to Chandigarh in 1994.
The legal and judicial administration of Chandigarh falls under the jurisdiction of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana.

blocks.content: Chandigarh became a Union Territory on 1 November 1966 under the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966, administered directly by the Central Government under Article 239 of the Constitution.

Uniquely among India's UTs, Chandigarh has no Lieutenant Governor of its own. Instead, since 1 June 1984, the Governor of Punjab has additionally held charge as the 'Administrator' of the UT — a dual role unlike any other Indian UT arrangement. Before 1984, Chandigarh had separate 'Chief Commissioners' as its administrative heads.

As of 2026, the Administrator is Shri Gulab Chand Kataria, who is concurrently the Governor of Punjab, in office since 31 July 2024. His official residence in Chandigarh is Punjab Raj Bhavan / Lok Bhavan.

Day-to-day administration is run by a Chief Secretary (an IAS officer) under the Administrator; as of 2026 this post is held by Shri H. Rajesh Prasad, appointed in October 2025. Below the Chief Secretary sit various Secretaries and Heads of Departments, largely drawn from the AGMUT (Arunachal Pradesh–Goa–Mizoram–Union Territories) cadre of the IAS.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: The Punjab & Haryana High Court is a rare case of one High Court simultaneously serving TWO states plus a Union Territory — a frequently tested distinguishing fact (compare with Bombay HC serving Maharashtra + Goa + Diu, Daman, D&NH).
Local Self-Government — Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh (MCC)

rows: Shared High Court of Punjab and Haryana

blocks.content: Urban local governance is handled by the Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh (MCC), established in 1994, headed by a Mayor elected annually (on a rotational basis among Councillors) rather than through direct public election of the Mayor's post itself.
The MCC is responsible for civic services — sanitation, water supply, roads maintenance, parks, and local taxation — across the city's sectors and the annexed villages/colonies.

Because Chandigarh has no rural Panchayati Raj structure of its own comparable to a full state (given its almost entirely urban/urbanising character), the MCC is the dominant tier of local governance, distinguishing it from most other Indian states/UTs which run a fuller three-tier Panchayati Raj system alongside urban bodies.

items: MCC elections are periodically held; results have oscillated between Congress, BJP and AAP-led coalitions in different terms, reflecting Chandigarh's politically competitive, cosmopolitan electorate.

The Mayor's post rotates annually among Councillors as per the Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1976 (as extended to Chandigarh) — meaning Chandigarh sees a new Mayor almost every year, a distinctive fact worth remembering for current-affairs-style questions on 'who is the current Mayor'.
The post of Chief Commissioner was replaced by the Governor of Punjab acting as Administrator of Chandigarh in May 1984.
The Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh (MCC) operates under the extension of the Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1976.
Chandigarh shares a common High Court with both Punjab and Haryana.
The Punjab & Haryana High Court at Chandigarh has appellate jurisdiction over both states and the UT — one of the busiest High Courts in India by case volume.

Chandigarh Police is a Commissionerate-system force headed by an Inspector General/Commissioner of Police, reporting to the UT Administration's Home Department (unlike many smaller towns which still use the district Superintendent of Police model).
UT since 1 Nov 1966; administered by the Governor of Punjab as ex-officio 'Administrator' since 1 June 1984 — Chandigarh has NO separate Lieutenant Governor.
Current (2026) Administrator: Gulab Chand Kataria (also Governor of Punjab), since 31 July 2024.
Chief Secretary (2026): H. Rajesh Prasad, IAS.
1 Lok Sabha seat; current MP (since 2024): Manish Tewari (INC). 0 Rajya Sabha seats.
Punjab & Haryana High Court, Chandigarh, serves BOTH neighbouring states plus the UT — a unique tri-jurisdiction arrangement.
Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh (MCC), est. 1994 — Mayor's post rotates annually among elected Councillors.
